content.text: Docker doesn't rebuild your image from scratch. It walks the Dockerfile from top to bottom and reuses each step from its build cache until one step has changed; from there, every later step runs again. Order instructions from least to most often changed, copy the lockfile before the source, and use a multi-stage build so the final image carries only what it needs to run.
A team's pull requests all wait on the same thing. Someone changes one line in a route handler, CI builds the Docker image, and the log shows

downloading every dependency again. On a laptop it's the same story: edit, rebuild, wait for packages that haven't changed. When someone suggests reordering the Dockerfile, the answer comes back quickly: it wouldn't help, because Docker rebuilds the whole image anyway.
The belief: the order of instructions in a Dockerfile doesn't affect build time, because every
starts from an empty image and runs every line. A Dockerfile reads like a shell script, and in a script the order decides whether it works, not how long the next run takes.

It's an honest conclusion from what people see. Both orders produce an image that works. And on many CI servers every build really does start cold: Docker's docs point out that in CI/CD pipelines "the builders are often ephemeral", which is why they recommend an external cache there. If your runner throws its cache away after each job, every build looks like a rebuild from scratch.
The half-truth: order doesn't change what the image does. It changes how much of the previous build Docker can reuse, and that's where the minutes go.
Every instruction is a cached step
Docker's cache docs say it plainly: "Each instruction in this Dockerfile translates to a layer in your final image." The article on images and layers showed that a
is a read-only stack of those layers. The builder keeps the result of every step in its
, and on the next build it goes through the Dockerfile in order, checking for each instruction whether it can reuse the stored result. When it can, the log says
and the step costs almost nothing.
The check depends on the instruction. For

, the builder "calculates a cache checksum from file metadata" of the copied files, and the cache is invalidated "if the file metadata has changed for any of the files involved." The modification time alone doesn't count: in our test, running
on the source files left every step
, the builder doesn't look at what the command would download or produce; "just the command string itself is used to find a match."
One miss invalidates everything below it

This is the rule that makes order matter: "Once the cache is invalidated, all subsequent Dockerfile commands generate new images and the cache isn't used." Later steps re-run "even if they wouldn't build anything differently." So with
near the top, any change anywhere in the project misses the cache at that line, and the
under it runs again. The docs' advice is to "order the instructions from less frequently changed to more frequently changed where possible."
Multi-stage builds separate building from running

instructions, and each one "begins a new stage of the build." You compile in one stage and copy only the output into the next, "leaving behind everything you don't want in the final image." The compiler, the type packages and the source files stay in the build stage. Each stage has its own steps in the cache, so the runtime stage's production install doesn't care when your source code changes.
The fix: dependencies first, source last
Here's a small Express API written in TypeScript, on

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
FROM node:24.22.2-alpine3.24
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm ci
RUN npm run build
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
FROM node:24.22.2-alpine3.24 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:24.22.2-alpine3.24
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

content.text: We built each version in its own copy of the project on Docker Desktop (Engine 29.4.3, BuildKit 0.29.0), changed one line in
, and built again. The output is trimmed to the steps that matter:

blocks.code:
docker build --progress=plain -t shop-api:wrong .
# #7 [3/5] COPY . .
# #7 DONE 0.2s
# #8 [4/5] RUN npm ci
# #8 DONE 44.1s
docker build --progress=plain -t shop-api:right .
# #8 [build 4/6] RUN npm ci
# #8 CACHED
# #10 [build 6/6] RUN npm run build
# #10 DONE 3.3s
# #11 [stage-1 4/5] RUN npm ci --omit=dev
# #11 CACHED
docker image ls --format '{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}' shop-api
# wrong 300MB
# right 255MB

content.text: In the wrong version, the edited file changed the checksum of
, so the install under it ran again. Across our runs a full
took between 3.8 and 44.1 seconds, depending on the network; on a real project it's whatever your full install costs. In the right version,

saw the same two files, so both installs came from the cache and only the TypeScript compile ran. The runtime image is also 45 MB smaller, because TypeScript and the type packages stayed behind in the build stage.

blocks.title: A cache hit can mean stale packages

content.text: The cache works against you for steps that fetch from the network. "The cache for

instructions isn't invalidated automatically between builds", so the docs warn that "rebuilding the image one week later will still get you the same packages as before." The best-practices guide says to "rebuild your images regularly with updated dependencies": run a scheduled build with
to get a fresh base image and fresh packages.
How to apply it in your project
Change one line of source code and build with
shows where your order breaks, and every step under it pays again.

items.title: Copy dependency files before the source

content.text: Copy only the files your package manager reads, such as
and the lockfile, then install, then
. The install now re-runs only when dependencies change.
Compile in a stage that has the SDK and dev dependencies, then start a second stage from a runtime image and copy in only the build output.

items.title: Give CI a cache to reuse

content.text: If your runners are ephemeral, export the cache with
, as Docker's docs recommend for CI/CD. Otherwise every job starts cold, whatever your order.

items.text: Docker reuses each Dockerfile step from its build cache until the first step that changed; every step after it runs again.
misses the cache when the copied files change, not when only their timestamps do;
misses only when its text or an earlier step changes.
Put what changes least at the top: copy the lockfile, install, then copy the source.
